title: After Childbirth: A Mother's Purification
summary: A woman who gives birth to a son is unclean for seven days, the boy is circumcised on the eighth day, and she then continues thirty-three days in purification; after the birth of a daughter the two periods are fourteen and sixty-six days. When her days are complete she brings a lamb for a burnt offering and a pigeon or turtledove for a sin offering, or two birds if she cannot afford a lamb, and the priest makes atonement for her so that she is clean.
story: Chapter 11 dealt with what Israel eats. Chapter 12 turns to the beginning of human life, and it is the first of the purity laws that concern the human body. Childbirth is the fulfillment of God's first blessing, to be fruitful and multiply (Genesis 1:28), and the Bible never treats it as shameful. Yet it also carries the mark of the fall, the pain of Genesis 3:16, and it involves the loss of blood, which in Leviticus always touches the boundary between life and death. This short chapter holds both realities together. It also mentions in passing the sign of God's covenant with Abraham, circumcision on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12). Centuries later a young mother from Nazareth would keep this law after the birth of her son, and Luke would record the offering she brought (Luke 2:22-24).
historical:
Childbirth was one of the most dangerous events in an ancient woman's life, and the Bible records its cost. Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin, naming him with her last breath (Genesis 35:17-18), and the wife of the priest Phinehas died in labor after hearing that the ark had been captured (1 Samuel 4:19-22). Births were attended by midwives (Genesis 35:17; Exodus 1:15-21). Circumcision itself was not unique to Israel. Jeremiah lists Egypt, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and desert peoples among those who practiced it (Jeremiah 9:25-26), while the Philistines were known as the uncircumcised (1 Samuel 17:26). What set Israel apart was the timing, on the eighth day of a boy's life rather than at puberty or marriage, and its meaning as the sign of God's covenant with Abraham's family.

This law lived on in Christian practice. The church remembers Mary's purification and the presentation of Jesus in the temple on February 2, forty days after Christmas, a feast long known in English as Candlemas. Many churches also kept a service of thanksgiving for a mother after childbirth, which the Book of Common Prayer called the Churching of Women, shaped more by gratitude for a safe delivery than by ideas of impurity.
cultural:
The mother's uncleanness came in two stages. For the first seven days after a son, or fourteen after a daughter, her status was like that during menstruation (15:19-24): what she lay or sat on became unclean, and so did anyone who touched it. In the longer second stage, most interpreters understand, she was no longer a source of impurity to others, but she could not touch holy things or enter the sanctuary. The forty days after a son broadly match the weeks of bleeding that normally follow a birth, and the second stage gave a new mother an extended time apart from the demands of public worship. Many traditional cultures still observe a postpartum rest of about forty days.

The offerings at the end mark her return to full participation in Israel's worship. The burnt offering expresses dedication to God. The sin offering, better understood here as a purification offering, does not imply that giving birth was sinful; it cleanses the effects of her impurity on the sanctuary and restores her to it. Both offerings are exactly the same whether she bore a son or a daughter (verses 6-7). The provision for a poor mother, two birds instead of a lamb and a bird (verse 8), repeats the mercy of 5:7.
literary: The chapter is one of the shortest in Leviticus, and it is carefully balanced. After the LORD's opening words (verses 1-2a), it sets the son (2-4) beside the daughter (5), gives the offerings that apply to both (6-7), and adds the provision for the poor (8). Verse 7 closes with a summary, “This is the law for a woman giving birth, whether to a male or to a female,” in the same style as the summaries that end other laws in this section (11:46-47; 13:59; 14:54-57; 15:32-33). The chapter also points ahead. It compares the mother's first stage to menstruation (verses 2 and 5), which is not regulated until chapter 15, a sign that these chapters were meant to be read together as one body of teaching. Jewish readers name the weekly reading that begins here Tazria, from the verb in verse 2 translated becomes pregnant, which literally means to produce seed.

outline.t: After the birth of a son: seven days, circumcision, and thirty-three days
After the birth of a daughter: fourteen days and sixty-six days
The offerings that complete her purification
Provision for a mother who cannot afford a lamb

doctrines.note: The chapter treats the birth of every child, son or daughter, as an event that brings the mother before God with offerings. The same offerings for both show that each child is received as a gift, and the provision for the poor ensures that no family is shut out.

Verse 3 mentions circumcision on the eighth day, the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:12). Every son born in Israel received the covenant sign within his first days, marking him as part of God's people before he could choose it.

Atonement here does not mean the mother sinned. The purification offering restores her after a season of impurity, reconnecting her with the sanctuary and the worshiping community. In Leviticus atonement covers both moral wrong and the defilement that comes simply from living in a mortal body.

words.note: Niddah, impurity, especially menstrual impurity. The root may mean to put away or to flee, reflecting the separation it involved. Later Jewish law uses the word as the name for the whole body of rules about menstruation and marriage, and a tractate of the Mishnah bears the name.

Tohar, purity or purification. The second stage of the mother's recovery is called the days of her purification (verses 4 and 6), a time of becoming clean rather than being unclean. The word points forward to restoration, not back to defilement.

Mul, to circumcise. It is used of the physical rite, and elsewhere the prophets and Moses call for a circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4), a people inwardly devoted to God. Paul takes up that language in Romans 2:29.

christ: Luke tells how Mary and Joseph kept this law. Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), and when the days of purification were complete they brought him to the temple with the sacrifice the law specified, “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24). That is the offering of verse 8, the provision for a mother who could not afford a lamb, so the Gospel quietly shows that Jesus was born into a poor household. Christians have often noticed the irony that the family of the one John would call “the Lamb of God” (John 1:29) could not afford a lamb. Paul sums up the scene when he writes that God sent his Son, “born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). The Son of God entered human life through the same bodily process this chapter regulates and was presented in the temple under the same law. The link is historical, not allegorical: Leviticus 12 is part of the ordinary life into which Jesus was born.

hard.q: Why does childbirth make a woman unclean, and why twice as long after a daughter?
hard.a:
Two misunderstandings need clearing away first. Impurity in Leviticus is not sin, and the offering does not imply guilt for bearing a child. Many scholars, following Jacob Milgrom, see the common thread in Leviticus 11 to 15 as the loss of life-carrying fluids and the nearness of death, which could not be brought into the presence of the living God. Childbirth, with its loss of blood, sits on that boundary even though it brings new life.

The doubled period after a daughter has no stated reason, and interpreters differ. Some see it as reflecting the lower social standing of women in the ancient world. Others suggest that the girl is herself a future mother, so her birth doubles the association with the mysteries of blood and life; some add that newborn girls occasionally have slight bleeding in their first days from their mothers' hormones. Others link the shorter period after a son to his circumcision on the eighth day, which marks a new stage. Whatever the reason, the chapter does not value the daughter less where it counts most: the offering for her birth is identical to the offering for a son, and the summary in verse 7 names both.

questions: The chapter holds together childbirth as blessing and as a brush with death. How have you seen both joy and fragility in the arrival of a child?
The law gave a new mother weeks away from public duties. What would it look like for a church to protect that kind of space for new parents today?
Jesus' family brought the poor person's offering. What does it tell you about God that his Son was born into a family that could not afford a lamb?
